<div class="ltx_page_content">

# Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability

<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"> <span class="ltx_personname">Alon Shakevsky </span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content"> <span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UC Berkeley  
shakevsky@berkeley.edu </span></span></span></span> <span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"> <span class="ltx_personname">Corban Villa </span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content"> <span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UC Berkeley </span></span></span></span> <span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"> <span class="ltx_personname">Ion Stoica </span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content"> <span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UC Berkeley </span></span></span></span> <span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"> <span class="ltx_personname">Raluca Ada Popa </span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content"> <span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>UC Berkeley </span></span></span></span>

</div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract">

###### Abstract

Discovering vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them requires high recall and reliable automatic validation, but existing approaches struggle to achieve both without prohibitive cost. We present Antiproof, an end-to-end vulnerability discovery system that combines *neuro-symbolic detector synthesis* for high-recall discovery with *proof-of-exploitability oracles* for automatic validation. Antiproof learns and iteratively refines static detectors from vulnerability datasets, then validates candidates by verifying whether executable proofs demonstrate concrete attacker capabilities. Evaluated on BountyBench and our curated KEVBench dataset, Antiproof detects 64 of 66 vulnerabilities, improving recall by more than 60 percentage points over static-analysis and neuro-symbolic baselines. In a scan of 50 widely deployed systems, Antiproof uncovered several hundred previously unknown vulnerabilities. We are responsibly disclosing all confirmed zero-days and have received 12 CVE assignments to date, including remote code execution vulnerabilities in Ray, SGLang, vLLM, and LiteLLM that could allow attackers to take over LLM training and inference systems.

</div>

<div id="S1" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Exploitable vulnerabilities are the most common initial-access vector in organizational data breaches \[<a href="#bib.bib13" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" class="ltx_ref">2</a>\] and the leading root cause of ransomware incidents \[<a href="#bib.bib14" class="ltx_ref">3</a>\]. Because the general problem of discovering such flaws is undecidable \[<a href="#bib.bib26" class="ltx_ref">4</a>\], practical systems must approximate and trade off <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">recall</span>, <span id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">precision</span>, and <span id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cost</span>. Addressing this tradeoff has become urgent as exploitation timelines have shrunk from years to hours \[<a href="#bib.bib33" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" class="ltx_ref">6</a>\], leaving defenders less time to discover and remediate vulnerabilities. An ideal solution for discovering exploitable flaws before attackers exploit them should provide high recall, reliable automatic validation (high precision), and low cost.

</div>

<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Automated vulnerability discovery has been extensively studied, but no existing method achieves these properties simultaneously across a broad range of vulnerability classes \[<a href="#bib.bib5" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" class="ltx_ref">8</a>\]. Static analysis tools can scan large systems \[<a href="#bib.bib55" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref">10</a>\], but require experts to specify vulnerability patterns and manually review findings. These tools often prioritize precision over recall to reduce false positives and review overhead \[<a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref">10</a>\]. Dynamic approaches, such as fuzzing and symbolic execution, are effective in finding memory-safety vulnerabilities, but do not easily generalize to vulnerability classes that lack reliable bug oracles. These approaches often become prohibitively expensive for scanning large systems due to path explosion and deep program states \[<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">14</a>\].

</div>

</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S1.T1.pic49" class="ltx_picture ltx_align_left ltx_figure_panel" /></span>
</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_break">

</div>
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p><span id="S1.T1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">, </span><span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S1.T1.pic50" class="ltx_picture" /></span><span id="S1.T1.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">, and </span><span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S1.T1.pic51" class="ltx_picture" /></span><span id="S1.T1.3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;"> denote full, partial, and no support, respectively. </span><sup><span id="S1.T1.3.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">*</span></sup><span id="S1.T1.3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">We do not evaluate proprietary systems because we do not have access to their source code, and we use public reports for comparison. </span><sup><span id="S1.T1.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">**</span></sup><span id="S1.T1.3.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Fuzzing and symbolic execution are limited to specific vulnerability classes, primarily memory safety.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE I: </span>Qualitative comparison of vulnerability discovery and validation systems.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">

Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong code-reasoning capabilities that can help address this challenge by automating parts of vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching \[<a href="#bib.bib5" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" class="ltx_ref">35</a>\]. Proprietary LLM agents, such as Claude Mythos \[<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" class="ltx_ref">36</a>\] and Codex Security \[<a href="#bib.bib32" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" class="ltx_ref">37</a>\], demonstrate that LLM-based systems can uncover thousands of vulnerabilities in production software. Despite this promise, LLM-based vulnerability discovery remains difficult to scale because LLM performance relies on careful context management \[<a href="#bib.bib67" class="ltx_ref">38</a>\], and a single project scan can require hundreds of millions of tokens and multiple days \[<a href="#bib.bib68" class="ltx_ref">39</a>\]. Continuous scanning is therefore impractical on large systems such as the Linux kernel. Moreover, high false-positive rates from LLM hallucinations and reward hacking create a validation bottleneck that requires expensive expert review to determine whether a finding is an exploitable vulnerability or a false positive \[<a href="#bib.bib68" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib66" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib75" class="ltx_ref">41</a>\]. For example, Anthropic reports running Claude Mythos roughly a thousand times on OpenBSD at a total cost of USD 20,000 and hiring security experts to manually validate its reports before disclosure \[<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref">23</a>\]. Recent work combines LLMs with static analysis \[<a href="#bib.bib63" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref">19</a>\], symbolic execution \[<a href="#bib.bib82" class="ltx_ref">29</a>\], and proof-of-concept generation \[<a href="#bib.bib62" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref">32</a>\], but remains limited to specific vulnerability classes or still requires manual expert review to validate exploitability. As shown in Table <a href="#S1.T1" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE I ‣ I Introduction ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>, these limitations motivate an end-to-end system that achieves high recall, automatic executable validation, and low cost.

</div>

<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">

In this work, we propose Antiproof, an end-to-end system that provides all three properties for a wide range of vulnerabilities. Our key insight, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, is to combine high-recall discovery with proofs of exploitability. To achieve this, we contribute two techniques: (1) Antiproof uses LLMs to synthesize reusable detectors and iteratively refine them for high-recall detection on a dataset of known vulnerabilities. To find vulnerabilities that data-flow analysis tools miss, including semantic vulnerabilities, we introduce eCPG traversals. An eCPG is a graph representation of code that extends the code property graph \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">42</a>\] with detector-specific virtual nodes and edges to support modeling new vulnerability classes. (2) Antiproof uses LLMs to create validation environments to validate the detected vulnerability candidates and generate proofs that demonstrate a concrete attacker capability, such as code execution, file access, SSRF, or authentication bypass. Antiproof implements proof-of-exploitability oracles that verify the proofs in a challenge-response protocol that rejects LLM hallucinations. This reduces vulnerability validation to proof search under a deterministic oracle.

</div>

<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">

Building a practical system from this insight raises three challenges:

</div>

<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">

1.  <span id="S1.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span></span>
    <div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

    <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detectors that generalize.</span> Synthesized detectors must capture the underlying vulnerability pattern rather than overfit to a specific vulnerability or project. Overly specific detectors may miss variants of the vulnerability class (low recall), while overly broad detectors produce too many candidates for validation (high validation cost). The system must generalize across project sizes, programming languages, frameworks, and vulnerability classes, including logic and semantic flaws that conventional static analysis struggles to express.

    </div>
2.  <span id="S1.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span></span>
    <div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

    <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Project-scale discovery.</span> Large systems with millions of lines of code, such as the Linux kernel, do not fit in a single LLM context window. The system must have high code coverage and construct only the minimal context that an LLM agent requires to validate each vulnerability candidate while avoiding prohibitive LLM inference cost.

    </div>
3.  <span id="S1.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span></span>
    <div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

    <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Exploitability validation.</span> LLMs can generate plausible but incorrect vulnerability reports and create a validation bottleneck that requires experts to manually review the reports. Automatic validation requires oracles that execute against the target system and check whether the vulnerability candidate enables an attacker-controlled security violation. These oracles must reject proofs that do not demonstrate practical risk to scale vulnerability validation.

    </div>

</div>

<span id="lstnumberx25.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx25.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">at</span><span id="lstnumberx25.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx25.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">state</span><span id="lstnumberx25.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">.</span><span id="lstnumberx25.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">c</span><span id="lstnumberx25.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">:1495,</span><span id="lstnumberx25.8" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx25.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">1514</span>
</div>

</div>
<div id="lstnumberx27" class="ltx_listingline">
<span id="lstnumberx27.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx27.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">at</span><span id="lstnumberx27.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx27.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">utility</span><span id="lstnumberx27.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">.</span><span id="lstnumberx27.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">c</span><span id="lstnumberx27.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">:1740</span>
</div>

</div>
<div id="lstnumberx29" class="ltx_listingline">
<span id="lstnumberx29.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx29.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">start_login</span><span id="lstnumberx29.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx29.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">via</span><span id="lstnumberx29.5" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx29.6" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">telnetd_setup</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 2: </span>Motivating example (simplified): <a href="https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2026-24061" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">CVE-2026-24061</a> in GNU InetUtils <span id="S1.F2.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">telnetd</span> allowed unauthenticated attackers to gain root access to over 212,000 internet-exposed devices. The root cause is that a remote attacker can set the <span id="S1.F2.20" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">USER</span> environment variable, which <span id="S1.F2.21" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">telnetd</span> injects unsanitized as an argument to the <span id="S1.F2.22" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">login</span> program. <span id="S1.F2.23" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span> the path from the attacker-controlled <span id="S1.F2.24" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">setenv</span> to the <span id="S1.F2.25" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">execv</span> sink, which traditional data-flow analysis (CodeQL, Joern) misses without a propagation model for the custom allocator (<span id="S1.F2.26" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">obstack</span>). <span id="S1.F2.27" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Middle:</span> eCPG detects the path from attacker-controlled input (<span id="S1.F2.28" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">net_read</span>) to a dangerous sink (<span id="S1.F2.29" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">execv</span>) and adds an observation about the <span id="S1.F2.30" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">setenv</span> write and <span id="S1.F2.31" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">getenv</span> read via a virtual edge. <span id="S1.F2.32" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> the context Antiproof prepares for the vulnerability candidate.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">

Antiproof addresses these challenges and manages the inherent tradeoff between recall, precision, and cost. The system refines vulnerability detectors for high recall rather than precision against a vulnerability dataset. Antiproof uses proofs of exploitability to shift the manual review bottleneck from every vulnerability candidate to a small set of validation environments and oracles. To run the synthesized detectors at scale, we implement Antigraph, a native engine that constructs the eCPG and evaluates detector traversals an order of magnitude faster than existing CPG tools (see Section <a href="#S5.SS5" class="ltx_ref" title="V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-E</span></a>), which allows Antiproof to continuously scan large systems without expensive LLM inference. This design aims to improve recall as the vulnerability dataset covers more patterns and as LLMs become more capable.

</div>

<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate Antiproof on known-vulnerability benchmarks and real-world zero-day discovery. We curate KEVBench, a dataset of CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">43</a>\] in 2025 and 2026. Antiproof detects 44 of 46 BountyBench \[<a href="#bib.bib3" class="ltx_ref">44</a>\] vulnerabilities and 20 of 20 KEVBench vulnerabilities, outperforming evaluated baselines by over 60 percentage points in recall. Across 50 widely deployed systems, Antiproof generated 510 proofs of exploitability. Due to time constraints, we selected 100 findings for manual review and coordinated disclosure. We have received 12 CVE assignments to date and discovered three vulnerabilities before their CVEs were publicly disclosed. Antiproof uncovered critical and high-severity flaws, including remote code execution vulnerabilities in Ray, SGLang, vLLM, and LiteLLM that allow attackers to take over LLM training and inference systems, steal GPU resources \[<a href="#bib.bib36" class="ltx_ref">45</a>\], and poison production LLM models.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Background</span>

<div id="S2.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Motivating Example</span>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

Consider <a href="https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2026-24061" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">CVE-2026-24061</a>, an authentication bypass vulnerability in GNU InetUtils <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">telnetd</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib58" class="ltx_ref">46</a>\] from CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">43</a>\] that allowed attackers to gain unauthenticated root access to over 212,000 internet-exposed devices. The root cause is that <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">telnetd</span> passed unsanitized user-controlled input to the <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">login</span> program and an attacker could inject an argument that skips password verification, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.

</div>

<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

Leading static analysis tools such as CodeQL \[<a href="#bib.bib57" class="ltx_ref">15</a>\] and Joern \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">42</a>\] miss this vulnerability without a propagation model for the custom allocator (<span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">obstack_grow</span>) that GNU InetUtils uses, which hides the flow between the source (<span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">getenv</span>) and the sink (<span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">execv</span>). Even with a complete model specified by an engineer or an LLM, taint analysis cannot verify whether the input is sufficiently sanitized. For example, <a href="https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2026-28372" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">CVE-2026-28372</a>, disclosed four weeks later, exploits the insufficient sanitization in the patch to <a href="https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2026-24061" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">CVE-2026-24061</a>. Since this vulnerability is not a memory-safety bug, approaches that rely on memory sanitizers \[<a href="#bib.bib72" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib71" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" class="ltx_ref">49</a>\], including fuzzing, are not effective in detecting it. This gap motivates our approach, which combines high-recall static detection with executable validation to discover and confirm such critical vulnerabilities.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Threat Model</span>

<figure id="S2.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S2.F3.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:104.9pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;">
<span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-190.0pt,57.8pt) scale(0.475899478981891,0.475899478981891) ;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S2.F3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span> </span>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 3: </span>Antiproof system architecture. <span id="S2.F3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span> learns high-recall heuristics from a vulnerability dataset and refines them from observed false positives and false negatives. <span id="S2.F3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection</span> runs the detectors on a target repository to find vulnerability candidates. <span id="S2.F3.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation</span> prepares a reusable PoE environment and a candidate-specific PoV environment, generates proofs, and checks each proof with its environment’s oracle.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We define the <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">attacker</span> as an untrusted actor interacting with the target system across a deployment trust boundary. As the systems under evaluation do not have precise definitions of their threat model, we use LLM agents to infer deployment configurations and trust boundaries from official documentation. We assume that the attacker controls inputs that a realistic deployment receives across a trust boundary, such as network requests, RPC messages, and serialized objects. We focus on systems where a validation environment can demonstrate exploitability using Docker containers, QEMU \[<a href="#bib.bib77" class="ltx_ref">50</a>\], or virtual machines.

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

We define an <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">exploitable vulnerability</span> as a software flaw that enables an attacker to gain a new capability on a deployed system or on a user’s system, such as code execution, file read, file write, authentication bypass, or denial of service. We do not consider flaws that do not enable new capabilities or are not reachable by the attacker as exploitable.

</div>

<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

We define a vulnerability as *known*, or *one-day*, if it is publicly tracked with a CVE or explicitly acknowledged in an official advisory or project documentation. We define a vulnerability as *previously unknown*, or *zero-day*, if it affects the latest release at the time of discovery and was not publicly documented when Antiproof found it.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">II-C</span> </span><span id="S2.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Code Property Graphs</span>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

A <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">code property graph</span> (CPG) is a graph representation of code that combines the abstract syntax tree, control-flow graph, and data-dependence graph into a single graph. CPGs have shown promise for modeling security vulnerabilities \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">42</a>\] with graph traversals \[<a href="#bib.bib79" class="ltx_ref">51</a>\]. Joern is an open-source tool that analyzes code through CPG queries and supports languages such as C/C++, Java, Python, JavaScript, PHP, and Go. In this work, we introduce extended CPG (eCPG) traversals to model vulnerabilities that are missed by data-flow analysis tools, such as CodeQL and Joern. Antiproof uses LLMs to generate and refine eCPG queries that detect a wide range of vulnerability classes.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS4" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">II-D</span> </span><span id="S2.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Proofs of Vulnerability and Exploitability</span>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We define a <span id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">proof of vulnerability</span> (PoV) as an executable test that uses a bug oracle, such as a test harness with assertions, to demonstrate a violation of a security property in isolation. The most widely deployed bug oracles are memory sanitizers \[<a href="#bib.bib71" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" class="ltx_ref">49</a>\], which detect memory-safety bugs by instrumenting a program such that a memory violation crashes the process. Bug oracles are effective for a limited set of vulnerability classes, but they do not generalize to vulnerability classes that lack a reliable bug oracle. They also require expert review to validate exploitability, since the test harness may require high privileges and the bug may not be an exploitable vulnerability (for example, system-level mitigations may prevent exploitation, and some bugs are challenging to exploit on their own, such as an out-of-bounds read of a single byte).

</div>

<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

We define a <span id="S2.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">proof of exploitability</span> (PoE) as an end-to-end test that demonstrates an attacker capability against a deployed system, such as code execution, file read or write, authentication bypass, or denial of service. In this work, we create validation environments and exploitability oracles to verify such a capability without requiring a precise bug oracle. PoEs must demonstrate an attack in a realistic environment and may require a chain of multiple vulnerabilities.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S2.SS5" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">II-E</span> </span><span id="S2.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs)</span>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">

The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">43</a>\] is a curated database maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) containing flaws that are actively exploited in real-world attacks, including data breaches and ransomware incidents. In this work, we curate a benchmark of KEVs to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in finding vulnerabilities with real-world impact.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S3" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Design</span>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">

Antiproof is designed to find exploitable vulnerabilities in large-scale systems with high recall, automatic validation (minimal manual review), and low inference and compute cost compared to direct LLM scanning. It consists of three subsystems: <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span>, <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection</span>, and <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation</span>, as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F3" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 3 ‣ II-B Threat Model ‣ II Background ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span> generates and refines static detectors once per vulnerability class, <span id="S3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection</span> runs them on a target repository to find vulnerability candidates, and <span id="S3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation</span> generates and checks a proof of vulnerability and a proof of exploitability for each candidate. Candidate detection and validation tasks are embarrassingly parallel, and Antiproof runs them with concurrent workers.

</div>

<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">

Antiproof scans generate the following three artifacts:

- <span id="S3.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Static hits.</span> Synthesized detectors detect vulnerability patterns from source code analysis.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proofs of vulnerability.</span> For each static hit, Antiproof generates an executable proof and accepts it only if the PoV environment’s crash oracle observes the target’s violation of the reported security property.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proofs of exploitability.</span> For each verified proof of vulnerability, Antiproof generates an executable proof that demonstrates an attacker capability and the proof-of-exploitability oracle verifies it.

  </div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">III-A</span> </span><span id="S3.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

The <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span> subsystem uses LLM agents to synthesize static detectors that identify vulnerability candidates in a target repository. Its design goal is to generate detectors that generalize across programming languages, frameworks, and vulnerability classes. To achieve this goal, Antiproof uses a vulnerability dataset that we curate from public vulnerability reports and fixes. The dataset includes vulnerable versions and ground-truth labels that specify vulnerable source code locations for recall measurement. Antiproof updates its detectors whenever a new vulnerability is added to the dataset.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

To scan large systems effectively, Antiproof refines the following three detectors:

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

1.  <span id="S3.I2.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span></span>
    <div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

    The <span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Scope</span> detector decomposes a repository into subsystems. Antiproof uses it to improve performance by building eCPGs for each subsystem rather than building one for an entire system, as smaller eCPGs are faster to analyze.

    </div>
2.  <span id="S3.I2.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span></span>
    <div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

    The <span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attack Surface</span> detector locates entry points that cross a trust boundary, including HTTP, RPC, and framework callbacks. Antiproof uses it to reduce the search space and focus on code paths that attackers can reach.

    </div>
3.  <span id="S3.I2.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span></span>
    <div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

    The <span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Candidates</span> detector searches for vulnerability candidates in paths that the attack surface reaches in each scoped eCPG. Each detector uses eCPG traversals to model a vulnerability class.

    </div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">

Rather than optimizing for precision, Antiproof optimizes for recall and reduces the resulting false positives with structural checks and iterative refinement. Each refinement round samples a detector’s hits, classifies false positives that do not fit the structural requirements of the vulnerability class, and fixes the detector until it achieves high recall (zero false negatives) with low noise (few false positives). Antiproof uses LLM agents and deterministic tests to verify that the detectors model a vulnerability class without overfitting to a specific CVE or project during synthesis.

</div>

The root cause is an asymmetry between a configuration reader and a writer. Antiproof adds a virtual node for the shared <span id="S3.F4.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">.git/config</span> resource, links the writer (<span id="S3.F4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">write_pair</span>) and reader (<span id="S3.F4.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">parse_value</span>) through it, and detects the asymmetry in their escape-character handling.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">III-B</span> </span><span id="S3.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection</span>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

The <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection</span> subsystem runs the synthesized detectors against the target repository. Detectors are heuristics for known vulnerability patterns that Antiproof optimizes for high recall and low noise. The synthesized detectors use eCPG traversals with detector-specific virtual edges and observations that over-approximate potential vulnerability candidates to achieve high recall.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

We demonstrate an example of effective detection via eCPG traversals of source-to-sink (taint-style) vulnerabilities. <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Source-to-sink</span> is a vulnerability pattern where attacker-controlled input (source) can reach a dangerous function call (sink). Figure <a href="#S1.F2" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows our motivating example, a KEV in <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">telnetd</span> that static taint analysis tools fail to detect without a custom taint propagation model. Antiproof overcomes this challenge by using breadth-first search (BFS) reachability instead of taint analysis: for every sink, it computes the set of methods that reach it, $R_{S}$, as well as the set of methods that can be reached from attacker-controlled entry points $R_{E}$, and adds the sink as a candidate if it is attacker-reachable, that is, ${R_{S} \cap R_{E}} \neq \varnothing$. For the motivating example, <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">net_read</span> reaches a <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">setenv</span> that writes the <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">USER</span> environment variable, and a <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">getenv</span> that reads the same <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">USER</span> variable reaches the <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">execv</span> sink. The detector links this write and read with a virtual edge over the shared variable, and uses eCPG traversals to detect the vulnerable flow. Antiproof additionally detects dynamic dispatch and polymorphism patterns in dynamic languages such as Python and JavaScript by over-approximating with BFS over eCPG virtual edges. As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F4" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 4 ‣ III-A Synthesis ‣ III Design ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, Antiproof uses eCPG traversals with virtual nodes and edges to detect semantic flaws that taint analysis cannot model.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

To achieve scalable continuous scanning, Antiproof uses several optimizations. First, since eCPG traversals use BFS rather than data-flow propagation, Antiproof avoids constructing the Program Dependence Graph (PDG), which is typically more expensive to construct than the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) or Control Flow Graph (CFG). Second, it extensively uses caching, for example to store the call graph, attack surface, and reachability trees. Third, it compiles the detectors and precomputes shared state. Finally, it uses a native engine rather than Joern, both to model languages that Joern does not support (such as Erlang) and to reduce scan time by an order of magnitude (Section <a href="#S5.SS5" class="ltx_ref" title="V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-E</span></a>).

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">III-C</span> </span><span id="S3.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation</span>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

The <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation</span> subsystem determines whether a vulnerability candidate is exploitable in a realistic target configuration. Antiproof prepares a validation environment that is reused across candidates with the same target configuration and oracle. For each candidate, it also prepares an instrumented PoV environment with a crash oracle. Antiproof generates PoVs and PoEs and checks each proof with its environment’s oracle. These validation environments can also be used to automatically validate candidates produced by other vulnerability detection systems.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Triage.</span> To manage the cost of LLM inference, Antiproof supports LLM-based triage of static analysis findings to deduplicate, rank, and classify findings. This allows Antiproof to prioritize realistic findings before investing in environment preparation or proof generation. The triage LLM agent can use the threat model of the system for classification, if available, to ignore findings outside of the threat model. The system can choose whether to remove findings, which may reduce recall, or to prioritize them within a budget.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Validation Environment Preparation.</span> Antiproof uses an LLM agent and reusable templates to prepare a reusable <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">validation environment</span> per target configuration to validate vulnerability candidates. A validation environment includes an execution environment, the deployed system, and a proof-of-exploitability oracle. The execution environment may be a Docker container (e.g., for web applications), a virtual machine with GPUs (e.g., for LLM inference serving), or an emulator such as QEMU (e.g., for operating system kernels such as Linux). Antiproof verifies that the deployed system version, dependencies, feature flags, and deployment options match the vulnerability candidate using deterministic verifiers. For each candidate, Antiproof also prepares a PoV environment with a crash oracle and instruments the system to crash when it detects a violation of the relevant security property via a runtime monitor implemented using memory sanitizers (for memory-safety bugs) and instrumented assertions (for other vulnerability classes). The assertions allow the runtime monitor to detect semantic flaws by crashing the program when the security invariant is violated. Antiproof refines the environments with feedback from an LLM verifier that checks consistency and realism.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proof Generation.</span> As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F5" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 5 ‣ III-C Validation ‣ III Design ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the validation environment runs the target system alongside an exploitability oracle, a small trusted program that checks a single attacker capability, for example, code execution, arbitrary file access, SSRF, authentication bypass, or service crash. The Prover, an LLM agent, generates and executes a proof against the validation environment. The oracle independently checks the resulting environment state and accepts the proof only if it demonstrates the required attacker capability. This validation is inspired by CTF (Capture The Flag) challenge validation \[<a href="#bib.bib4" class="ltx_ref">52</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" class="ltx_ref">53</a>\], such as kernelCTF \[<a href="#bib.bib83" class="ltx_ref">54</a>\], which verifies whether an attacker can achieve code execution on the Linux kernel. We extend the notion of CTF validation to capability-based challenges that prove attacker primitives beyond code execution and crashes. With a deterministic verifier, proof generation becomes a search problem, allowing LLMs or fuzzers to validate vulnerabilities beyond memory safety and capabilities beyond code execution.

</div>

<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S3.F5.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:186.7pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;">
<span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(41.8pt,-22.6pt) scale(1.31933591362351,1.31933591362351) ;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S3.F5.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span> </span>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 5: </span>An exploitability oracle as a challenge–response protocol. The oracle generates a challenge in the validation environment. The Prover, an LLM agent, connects over the network and executes a proof of exploitability against the target system. The oracle then verifies the state of the validation environment and accepts the proof if and only if the observed response correctly solves the challenge.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S3.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">

Proof-of-exploitability validation shifts the review bottleneck from each vulnerability candidate to a smaller set of trusted oracles (once per capability) and reusable validation environments (once per target configuration). A single exploitability oracle can automatically validate many vulnerabilities and save manual review effort. A vendor that trusts a validation environment can use it to automatically validate vulnerabilities in their system, similar to how Google automatically validates Linux kernel vulnerability reports using kernelCTF (but not limited to code execution).

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p6" class="ltx_para">

To ensure that proof-of-exploitability oracles accept a proof if and only if it demonstrates the attacker capability, we carefully review them using LLM agents and manual review. Antiproof implements exploitability oracles that use a cryptographically secure secret $s$ and a mounted challenge directory <span id="S3.SS3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge</span>, for example:

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p7" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="S3.I3.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Arbitrary Code Execution.</span> The oracle generates $s$, ensures that <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span> does not exist, creates a script <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/rce.sh</span> such that executing the script would write the secret $s$ into <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span> (e.g., <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">echo "\$secret" \> /challenge/secret</span>), then accepts a proof if and only if $s$ is indeed written to <span id="S3.I3.i1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span>.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I3.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Arbitrary File Read.</span> The oracle generates $s$ and stores it in <span id="S3.I3.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span>, then accepts a proof if and only if it returns $s$.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I3.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Arbitrary File Write.</span> The oracle generates $s$, ensures <span id="S3.I3.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span> does not exist, and provides it to the prover, then accepts a proof if and only if $s$ is indeed written to <span id="S3.I3.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/challenge/secret</span>.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I3.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Server-Side Request Forgery.</span> The oracle generates $s$ and provides it to the prover, runs a listener in the validation environment, and registers the listener’s host under a list of aliases on the environment network. It accepts a proof if and only if the listener receives $s$ from the target rather than directly from the prover.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I3.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Authentication Bypass.</span> The oracle generates $s$ and places a proxy in front of the protected endpoints that returns $s$ when a request reaches a protected endpoint without authentication. The oracle accepts if and only if $s$ appears in the proof’s output.

  </div>
- <span id="S3.I3.i6"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S3.I3.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S3.I3.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Denial of Service.</span> The oracle verifies a proof by checking whether the target has crashed (e.g., its process has died), become unavailable (e.g., its health check fails), or failed to terminate (and is killed after a timeout).

  </div>

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p8" class="ltx_para">

Formally, let $E$ be a validation environment, let $C$ be an attacker capability (primitive), and let $\pi$ be a candidate executable proof. We define the oracle $O_{C}$ as:

|     |                                                                       |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     | $${O_{C}\hspace{0pt}{(E,\pi)}} = \begin{cases}                        
       1 & {\text{if~}\pi\text{~demonstrates~}C\text{~against~}E\text{,}} \\  
       0 & \text{otherwise.}                                                  
       \end{cases}$$                                                          |     |

A rejected proof, ${O_{C}\hspace{0pt}{(E,\pi)}} = 0$, does not imply the absence of $C$, only that the specific proof failed to demonstrate it. The exploitability oracles are independent of vulnerability classes by construction and depend only on the capability $C$ and the validation environment $E$. The oracles are sound if the security games accurately model the system and every accepted proof demonstrates the capability.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p9" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S3.SS3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oracle threat model.</span> The exploitability oracle and validation environment are trusted and manually reviewed, while the prover is an untrusted attacker that connects to the target over the network. Each challenge uses a cryptographically secure secret and access-controlled challenge state. We manually review every validation environment to ensure that the prover cannot generate a proof that the oracle accepts without demonstrating the attacker capability, as guessing the secret has negligible success probability.

</div>

<div id="S3.SS3.p10" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S3.SS3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oracle coverage.</span> A single exploitability oracle can validate many different vulnerabilities. For example, the Arbitrary Code Execution oracle can validate 9 of the 2025 Top 10 KEV vulnerability classes, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE II ‣ III-C Validation ‣ III Design ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>, including unsafe deserialization, OS command injection, and code injection vulnerabilities. It does not currently support client-side vulnerabilities such as cross-site scripting (XSS), since client-side code may be attacker-controlled. Because there are fewer exploitability oracles than vulnerability classes, manual review can focus on verifying the correctness of a small set of validation environments and automatically validate any vulnerability that is accepted by the exploitability oracles.

</div>

<div id="S4" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Implementation</span>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We implemented our approach to support interchangeable static detectors and LLM agents. The static detectors output SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) and the LLM agents output structured JSON. Antiproof uses a PostgreSQL database and a web interface to store and deduplicate findings and track triage decisions, validation results, and disclosure status.

</div>

<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Static Detectors.</span> Antiproof synthesizes static detectors and refines them to be high-recall heuristics that approximate vulnerability candidates. It supports two eCPG query engines: (1) Joern, which executes queries as Scala scripts using a Java Virtual Machine (JVM) per invocation, and (2) Antigraph, our native Rust eCPG engine implementation. Antigraph partially implements the CPG specification \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib80" class="ltx_ref">56</a>\] but does not construct the expensive Program Dependence Graph (PDG). It implements language frontends using <span id="S4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tree-sitter</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib78" class="ltx_ref">57</a>\], including languages that Joern does not officially support, such as Erlang. Antiproof automatically detects subsystems, builds a CPG for each subsystem, and detects candidates using the selected eCPG engine.

</div>

<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Detector coverage.</span> Antiproof’s 32 synthesized detectors cover 45 vulnerability classes, including 9 of the 10 most actively exploited weakness classes, as shown in Table <a href="#S3.T2" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE II ‣ III-C Validation ‣ III Design ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>. The current implementation does not yet cover client-side classes such as cross-site scripting, which we leave to future work.

</div>

<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agents.</span> Antiproof supports any LLM agent, including harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex. The system enforces structured outputs (JSON) using <span id="S4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pydantic</span> schemas and iterative refinement with verifier feedback. Agents are given a shell tool in a Docker container with language runtimes installed (e.g., Python 3.12, JDK 21, Erlang/OTP, Codex CLI 0.128.0, and Claude Code CLI 2.1.132 pre-installed), with <span id="S4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/code</span> mounted read-only and <span id="S4.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/workspace</span> writable and reset between candidates.

</div>

<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Validation Environments.</span> Antiproof implements validation environments using Docker containers, QEMU (e.g., for operating system emulation), or virtual machines (e.g., GPUs for inference serving). Each exploitability oracle generates a challenge for one attacker capability and checks whether the LLM-generated proof solves it. Antiproof creates a container for generated proofs and connects it to the validation environment through a Docker network or SSH forwarding. For PoVs, Antiproof uses the crash oracle and creates a candidate-specific PoV environment with assertions that crash when the vulnerability is detected.

</div>

<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S4.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vulnerability Dataset.</span> We implemented scripts that collect vulnerability reports from GitHub Security Advisories, bug bounty writeups, and fix commits. We collected over 400 CVE reports in the evaluated projects to analyze common vulnerability patterns. For recall measurement, we collect the reports of the benchmark vulnerabilities and generate ground-truth labels for static detection that score a hit based on line proximity or enclosing method.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Evaluation</span>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate Antiproof using the following research questions:

</div>

<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">

- <span id="S5.I1.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ1.</span> What recall does Antiproof achieve on known exploitable vulnerabilities? (Section <a href="#S5.SS3" class="ltx_ref" title="V-C RQ1: Known-Vulnerability Detection ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-C</span></a>)

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I1.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ2.</span> Can Antiproof discover previously unknown vulnerabilities? (Section <a href="#S5.SS4" class="ltx_ref" title="V-D RQ2: Zero-Day Discovery ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-D</span></a>)

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I1.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ3.</span> How efficient is Antiproof at scanning large systems? (Section <a href="#S5.SS5" class="ltx_ref" title="V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-E</span></a>)

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I1.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RQ4.</span> Which components contribute to recall and cost? (Section <a href="#S5.SS6" class="ltx_ref" title="V-F RQ4: Component Contributions ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-F</span></a>)

  </div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS1" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">V-A</span> </span><span id="S5.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Experimental Setup</span>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">

All experiments run on a GCP <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">n2-highmem-32</span> instance (32 vCPUs, 256 GB RAM) provisioned via SkyPilot \[<a href="#bib.bib49" class="ltx_ref">58</a>\]. Experiments that include end-to-end validation that requires GPUs, for example inference engines, additionally use GCP <span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">g2-standard-4</span> instances with one NVIDIA L4 GPU.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span> For RQ1, our primary comparisons are open-source static-analysis and neuro-symbolic tools. We run the baselines in Docker containers that mount the target at <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/code</span> and write tool outputs to <span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/workspace</span>. We score each baseline by the number of findings that are semantically equivalent to the benchmark ground-truth vulnerability reports. We compare recall against the following baselines:

- <span id="S5.I2.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Semgrep</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib69" class="ltx_ref">16</a>\]. Semgrep is an open-source static analysis tool that scans code for security vulnerabilities using predefined rules. We use the open-source <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">semgrep/semgrep</span> Docker image and run <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">semgrep scan</span> with <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">--config=auto</span>, <span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">--no-git-ignore</span>, and JSON output.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I2.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CodeQL</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib57" class="ltx_ref">15</a>\]. CodeQL is a semantic code analysis engine that models vulnerabilities as queries over program structure and data flow. We use GitHub CodeQL CLI 2.25.5, create databases with <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">autobuild</span>, and run the language-specific <span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">security-extended</span> query suite.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I2.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RepoAudit</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib45" class="ltx_ref">21</a>\]. RepoAudit is an LLM-guided repository-auditing system for source-to-sink bug patterns. We run its <span id="S5.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">dfbscan</span> mode with reachability enabled, temperature 0, and call depth 3. RepoAudit only supports three vulnerability classes (null-pointer dereference, memory leak, and use-after-free).

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I2.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  <span id="S5.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">KNighter</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref">19</a>\]. KNighter synthesizes static-analysis checkers from vulnerability-fixing commits. KNighter only supports Linux-kernel vulnerabilities and struggles with use-after-free vulnerabilities that require state-machine and concurrency reasoning. In our benchmarks, this leaves only one supported target, the Linux use-after-free KEV. We provide KNighter with similar vulnerability patches and measure whether the generated detector can find the Linux KEV.

  </div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">

We also include direct LLM scanning reference points using Codex with <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.3-codex</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.4-mini</span>, and <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.5</span>, and Claude Code with <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude-opus-4.6</span>. We include <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude-opus-4.6</span> because Anthropic uses it in their published large-scale zero-day discovery evaluation in open-source software \[<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" class="ltx_ref">60</a>\]. These agents are not primary baselines because their performance depends strongly on model choice, prompt engineering, and inference budget. We run each agent in a Docker container with its CLI, Python 3.12, <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">git</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ripgrep</span>, <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">jq</span>, and <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">uv</span>. The target repository is mounted read-only at <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/code</span> with a writable <span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">/workspace</span>. The read-only mount prevents the agent from modifying the project’s code, and the workspace allows the agent to save proof-of-concept artifacts and temporary files. As shown in Appendix <a href="#A1" class="ltx_ref" title="Appendix A Agent Prompts ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>, we use prompts that instruct the agent to find all vulnerabilities in a candidate file and to report each finding with a proof-of-concept reproduction, similar to the approach described by Anthropic for their zero-day scans \[<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref">59</a>\]. We do not evaluate Claude Code Security or Codex Security because their terms of service do not allow scanning third-party repositories.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">

We allow 30 minutes per target and run each configuration 10 times. Table <a href="#S5.T3" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE III ‣ V-B Metrics ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a> shows the mean detections rounded to the nearest vulnerability and total recall percentages computed from the unrounded means.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">V-B</span> </span><span id="S5.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Metrics</span>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">

We use the following metrics in our evaluation:

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Recall.</span> For known vulnerabilities, we measure <span id="S5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">recall</span> as the fraction of benchmark vulnerabilities for which the system detects the ground-truth vulnerability.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hits, PoVs, and PoEs.</span> For zero-day discovery, we track the funnel of *Hits* (static-detector candidates), *PoVs* (proofs of vulnerability that the crash oracle accepts in a candidate-specific PoV environment), and *PoEs* (proofs of exploitability accepted by the exploitability oracle).

</div>

<div id="S5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cost.</span> We measure the time and cost in USD of candidate discovery (CPG construction and static detector execution) and automatic validation (environment preparation, environment execution, and LLM inference).

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">V-C</span> </span><span id="S5.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RQ1: Known-Vulnerability Detection</span>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate Antiproof on known-vulnerability benchmarks to measure recall. First, we evaluate on BountyBench, a public benchmark of real-world bug-bounty vulnerabilities. To reduce data-contamination risk and focus on exploitable vulnerabilities with real-world impact, we additionally curate KEVBench, a dataset of CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">43</a>\] that became public in 2025 and 2026, after the knowledge cutoff of some of the LLMs we use in our evaluation.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmark scope.</span> We measure recall on vulnerability detection, where the system generates vulnerability reports given a project. We do not evaluate on CyberGym \[<a href="#bib.bib2" class="ltx_ref">61</a>\] because its primary task is proof-of-concept reproduction from a vulnerability description, and its benchmark is centered on memory-safety bugs in fuzzing-style targets, while we focus on broad vulnerability-class coverage beyond memory safety.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BountyBench.</span> BountyBench \[<a href="#bib.bib3" class="ltx_ref">44</a>\] contains real-world vulnerabilities from 25 open-source projects, curated from public bug bounty programs with disclosed awards totaling over USD 60,000. To the best of our knowledge, the highest previously reported detection rate on BountyBench is Co-RedTeam’s 20% result with <span id="S5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Gemini-3-pro</span> \[<a href="#bib.bib35" class="ltx_ref">22</a>\]. We use BountyBench as a known-vulnerability target set by collecting its CVEs, checking out the affected project versions, and scoring whether each system reports a finding semantically equivalent to the ground-truth vulnerability. Antiproof detects 44 of 46 BountyBench vulnerabilities (96%).

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">KEVBench.</span> We curate KEVBench from CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities \[<a href="#bib.bib34" class="ltx_ref">43</a>\] (KEVs) catalog by selecting 2025 and 2026 KEVs that affect open-source projects. The resulting benchmark contains 20 exploited-in-the-wild vulnerabilities across 12 vulnerability classes, 7 programming languages, and 17 projects.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> As shown in Table <a href="#S5.T3" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE III ‣ V-B Metrics ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>, Antiproof detects 64 of 66 vulnerabilities with <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.5</span>, outperforming the strongest primary baseline, Semgrep, by 71 percentage points and the strongest direct LLM-agent reference point by 38 percentage points. It detects 62, 61, 60, or 59 of 66 using <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.3-codex</span>, <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">claude-opus-4.6</span>, <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen 3.7-Max</span>, or <span id="S5.SS3.p5.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GLM-5.1</span>, respectively. Because direct LLM scanning depends on the model, prompt, tool setup, and inference budget, we do not claim that LLM agents cannot find these vulnerabilities. Antiproof is complementary to direct LLM scanning because its static detectors can guide LLM agents during search, and its exploitability oracles can validate findings produced by those agents.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS4" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">V-D</span> </span><span id="S5.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RQ2: Zero-Day Discovery</span>

<figure id="S5.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div id="S5.F6.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:132.6pt;vertical-align:-0.0pt;">
<span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(41.1pt,-15.8pt) scale(1.31260413861311,1.31260413861311) ;"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S5.F6.pic1" class="ltx_picture" /></span> </span>
</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 6: </span>End-to-end zero-day discovery funnel across 50 scanned projects.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">

We evaluate Antiproof on 50 widely deployed open-source projects. We select projects with high security impact on AI and cloud infrastructure, including LLM training and inference systems, that can be emulated in Docker containers, QEMU, or virtual machines. The selected projects total 136 million lines of code across 8 languages, with an average of 2.7 million lines per project and a maximum of 31.5 million lines.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> In our initial zero-day scan, Antiproof found 17,574 vulnerability candidates, generated 1,212 PoVs, and accepted 510 PoEs (Figure <a href="#S5.F6" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 6 ‣ V-D RQ2: Zero-Day Discovery ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Due to time constraints, we selected 100 findings for manual review and coordinated disclosure. Antiproof has uncovered critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including remote code execution in LLM training and inference systems, and denial-of-service and potential code-execution flaws in critical infrastructure such as OpenSSL and FreeBSD. We have received 12 CVE assignments to date and confirmed three vulnerabilities before their CVEs were publicly disclosed. We continue to improve the static detectors in recall and precision and to scale the validation environments. Table <a href="#S5.T4" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE IV ‣ V-D RQ2: Zero-Day Discovery ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a> reports the per-project language, size, funnel, and cost.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cost reference.</span> Anthropic reports that the OpenBSD campaign that found the SACK vulnerability ran Mythos roughly a thousand times at a total cost of USD 20,000 \[<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref">23</a>\]. Antiproof validated its static findings in OpenBSD with <span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.3-codex</span> for less than USD 612, a $33 \times$ lower cost, and reproduces the Mythos findings, SACK null-dereference in OpenBSD and FreeBSD <a href="https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2026-4747" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">CVE-2026-4747</a>, for USD 0.46 and USD 1.73, respectively. These costs reflect a single run of an early prototype and represent an upper bound, as we have continued to optimize the system since the scan.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">V-E</span> </span><span id="S5.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability</span>

<figure id="S5.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<span class="ltx_inline-block"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," id="S5.F7.pic1" class="ltx_picture ltx_centering" /></span>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 7: </span>Detector efficiency and scalability on KEVBench and BountyBench.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">

Continuous scanning of large systems requires fast detection that scales with project size. We compare Antigraph, Antiproof’s native eCPG engine, against Joern on the full 66-target KEV and BountyBench set. Both engines run with a cold cache, rebuilding all graphs in every iteration, and reach identical recall (64 of 66).

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Throughput.</span> As Figure <a href="#S5.F7" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 7 ‣ V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>(a) shows, Antigraph scans all benchmark targets 25$\times$ faster than Joern, a median of 2.3 versus 59 minutes across 5 trials.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scaling.</span> As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 7 ‣ V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>(b), Antigraph’s median per-target time is 27.3 s, 92$\times$ faster than Joern’s 2,505 s, with a maximum of 140 s on the largest target, the Linux kernel at 51k scoped files.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Time breakdown.</span> As shown in Figure <a href="#S5.F7" class="ltx_ref" title="Fig. 7 ‣ V-E RQ3: Detector Efficiency and Scalability ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>(c), Joern spends 92% of its run time building and loading CPGs. By contrast, Antigraph is 25$\times$ faster, as it avoids building the expensive program-dependence graph via BFS reachability in Rust over the eCPG rather than Joern’s data-flow propagation in Scala.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S5.SS6" class="section ltx_subsection">

### <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS6.6" class="ltx_text">V-F</span> </span><span id="S5.SS6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">RQ4: Component Contributions</span>

<div id="S5.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">

We run the following ablations to measure how Antiproof’s components contribute to recall and cost:

- <span id="S5.I3.i1"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">

  $-$<span id="S5.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">eCPG</span> replaces Antiproof’s reachability traversal with Joern’s native data-flow reachability, <span id="S5.I3.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">reachableByFlows</span>.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I3.i2"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">

  $-$<span id="S5.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">eCPG frontends</span> disables the custom eCPG frontends that Antiproof implements for languages Joern cannot ingest natively, namely Erlang and Velocity.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I3.i3"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

  $-$<span id="S5.I3.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attack Surface</span> disables the detector that selects attacker-facing entry points.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I3.i4"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I3.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">

  $-$<span id="S5.I3.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scope</span> disables repository-scope detection and builds whole-repository CPGs.

  </div>
- <span id="S5.I3.i5"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span></span>
  <div id="S5.I3.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">

  $-$<span id="S5.I3.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">observations</span> removes technique facts and structural observations from the prover prompt.

  </div>

Static detector runs use a 20-minute per-target timeout.

</div>
