<td id="S5.T5.2.1.9.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.9.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">51</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.9.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.9.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">–</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.9.6" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.9.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">–</span></td>
</tr>
<tr id="S5.T5.2.1.10" class="even ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_left"> <span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span class="math inline">−</span><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">observations</span></span> <span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">(</span><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">gpt-5.5</span><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.1.1.2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">, medium)</span></span> </span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">41</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">19</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">60</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">–</span></td>
<td id="S5.T5.2.1.10.6" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding: 0.55pt 2.0pt"><span id="S5.T5.2.1.10.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">–</span></td>

</div>
<figcaption><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE V: </span>Component ablation study.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div id="S5.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S5.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Results.</span> The <span id="S5.SS6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Detection ablations</span> in Table <a href="#S5.T5" class="ltx_ref" title="TABLE V ‣ V-F RQ4: Component Contributions ‣ V Evaluation ‣ Antiproof: Synthesizing Vulnerability Detectors and Proofs of Exploitability"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a> show that each component improves recall or efficiency. Antiproof with eCPG detects 18 more benchmark vulnerabilities than Joern’s native data-flow reachability and runs 25$\times$ faster. The custom eCPG frontends for Erlang and Velocity recover two KEVBench vulnerabilities that Joern’s native frontends cannot parse. Scope detection reduces the candidate count by 80% and scan time by 3.3$\times$ by focusing CPG construction on relevant code, while maintaining recall. Attack Surface detection reduces the candidate count by 31% and scan time by 2.1$\times$ while maintaining recall.

</div>

<div id="S5.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">

The <span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Validation ablations</span> show that the static observations improve recall. Removing observations with <span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.3-codex</span> at medium effort detects 36 of 46 BountyBench targets and 15 of 20 KEVBench targets, for 51 of 66 total. With <span id="S5.SS6.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-5.5</span> at medium effort, the system detects 41 of 46 BountyBench targets and 19 of 20 KEVBench targets, for 60 of 66 total.

</div>

</div>

</div>

<div id="S6" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Discussion and Limitations</span>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vulnerability Detectors.</span> Antiproof can only find vulnerabilities that the synthesized detectors detect. Because the system synthesizes detectors from known vulnerability patterns, it may miss a novel pattern until it learns a corresponding detector. To mitigate such false negatives, Antiproof can synthesize new detectors from additional known vulnerabilities or generate candidates with external systems, such as LLM agents or other static analysis tools. Moreover, Antiproof uses synthesized detectors that detect scope and attack surface to avoid path explosion, which may lead to false negatives if a real vulnerability is outside of the detected paths. Antiproof mitigates this by testing its detectors on a wide range of projects across different programming languages and frameworks.

</div>

<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Static Analysis Tools.</span> Antiproof depends on the quality of its static detectors and eCPG engines. It supports two engines, Joern and Antigraph, which must correctly parse the source languages, build the eCPG, and execute its traversals. Any error in these steps can cause Antiproof to miss vulnerabilities.

</div>

<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">End-to-end validation.</span> Automatic vulnerability validation requires environments that accurately simulate the target system. PoV environments are candidate-specific, whereas a validation environment can be reviewed once and reused across candidates. Our evaluation focuses on open-source projects because Antiproof assumes source-code access for analysis and validation. We leave scanning proprietary systems to future work. In some cases, accurate simulation may be challenging, for example, when hardware emulation or third-party authentication is required, which may lead to false positives or false negatives. Our proof-of-exploitability oracles cover the attacker primitives evaluated in this paper, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SSRF, authentication bypass, and denial of service. Vulnerabilities whose impact does not map cleanly to these primitives may require experts to create and manually review new exploitability oracles.

</div>

<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threat Model.</span> Antiproof may generate reports for exploitable vulnerabilities that are outside the threat model of the target system. To mitigate that, we use LLMs to generate and update a threat model document. Antiproof uses the threat model document to classify and prioritize findings. Future work may improve the accuracy of these LLM-generated threat models, allowing Antiproof to focus on in-scope findings and reduce cost and false positives. In some cases, project maintainers may dispute real vulnerabilities and consider them out of scope or without security impact, while real-world attackers exploit them in the wild \[<a href="#bib.bib36" class="ltx_ref">45</a>\].

</div>

<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM limitations.</span> Antiproof uses LLMs to synthesize detectors, generate proof-of-vulnerability (PoV) tests, set up validation environments, and generate proofs of exploitability (PoE). Generating a PoE may be challenging or require a chain of multiple vulnerabilities. The model may also refuse cybersecurity tasks such as exploitation due to safety filters. To reduce these false negatives, Antiproof supports any LLM agent, including open-weight models, and can run multiple agents with different providers. To reduce false positives, we manually review the exploitability oracles and validation environments.

</div>

<div id="S6.p6" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S6.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Threats to validity.</span> As our known-vulnerability benchmarks, BountyBench and KEVBench, are publicly available, LLM agents may memorize the vulnerabilities or exploits from their training data or discover them via web search. To mitigate this risk of data contamination, KEVBench uses known exploited vulnerabilities that became public in 2025 and 2026, after the knowledge cutoff of some of the LLMs we evaluate. To reduce the risk of memorization, we additionally evaluate Antiproof’s effectiveness in zero-day discovery. Exact reproduction of our experiments that use proprietary LLM models may be challenging, as their performance can depend on the model capabilities and safety filters. To reduce this risk, Antiproof supports open-weight models, such as <span id="S6.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GLM-5.1</span>.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S7" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Program Analysis.</span> Program analysis approaches for vulnerability discovery, such as static analysis \[<a href="#bib.bib55" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" class="ltx_ref">10</a>\], fuzzing \[<a href="#bib.bib51" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib52" class="ltx_ref">14</a>\], taint analysis \[<a href="#bib.bib53" class="ltx_ref">62</a>\], and symbolic execution \[<a href="#bib.bib48" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" class="ltx_ref">12</a>\], have been extensively studied. Query-based approaches, such as CodeQL \[<a href="#bib.bib57" class="ltx_ref">15</a>\] and code property graphs \[<a href="#bib.bib8" class="ltx_ref">42</a>\], are effective for specific vulnerability patterns, but rely on expert-written models, source and sink specifications, and manual validation of alerts. Fuzzing and symbolic execution are effective for vulnerability discovery and automatic exploit generation \[<a href="#bib.bib81" class="ltx_ref">63</a>\], but are primarily limited to memory safety and struggle with harness engineering, exponential search spaces, and deep program states. Arbiter \[<a href="#bib.bib74" class="ltx_ref">28</a>\] and SAILOR \[<a href="#bib.bib82" class="ltx_ref">29</a>\] combine static analysis with symbolic execution to discover specific memory safety vulnerabilities. In contrast, Antiproof detects vulnerabilities beyond memory-safety and combines neuro-symbolic static analysis for high-recall detection with proofs of exploitability for automatic validation.

</div>

<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM-Based Static Analysis.</span> Prior work uses LLMs to guide vulnerability classification with code property graphs (LLMxCPG \[<a href="#bib.bib9" class="ltx_ref">64</a>\]) and to infer specifications for taint-based vulnerabilities in Java (IRIS \[<a href="#bib.bib47" class="ltx_ref">17</a>\], Argus \[<a href="#bib.bib65" class="ltx_ref">65</a>\]), PHP (Artemis \[<a href="#bib.bib59" class="ltx_ref">66</a>\]), and JavaScript (SemTaint \[<a href="#bib.bib64" class="ltx_ref">67</a>\]). Recent work explores neuro-symbolic static analysis, where LLMs synthesize static detectors from historical vulnerability patterns, including C/C++ static analyzers (KNighter \[<a href="#bib.bib37" class="ltx_ref">19</a>\]), CodeQL queries (QLCoder \[<a href="#bib.bib60" class="ltx_ref">18</a>\]), and Joern queries (MoCQ \[<a href="#bib.bib63" class="ltx_ref">20</a>\]). ProtocolGuard \[<a href="#bib.bib76" class="ltx_ref">68</a>\] combines LLM-guided static analysis with dynamic verification to detect protocol non-compliance bugs. In comparison, Antiproof introduces eCPG traversals to detect vulnerabilities that prior approaches fail to model, including semantic vulnerabilities, synthesizes static detectors and refines them for high recall on a wide range of vulnerability classes, and uses proof-of-exploitability oracles for automatic validation rather than expert review or LLM verifiers.

</div>

<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agentic Vulnerability Discovery.</span> LLM agents have shown promise for vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching \[<a href="#bib.bib44" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" class="ltx_ref">70</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" class="ltx_ref">72</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" class="ltx_ref">73</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib61" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" class="ltx_ref">75</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" class="ltx_ref">61</a>, <a href="#bib.bib70" class="ltx_ref">76</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" class="ltx_ref">77</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" class="ltx_ref">78</a>, <a href="#bib.bib56" class="ltx_ref">35</a>\]. Proprietary systems including Claude Mythos \[<a href="#bib.bib30" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" class="ltx_ref">36</a>\], Claude Code Security \[<a href="#bib.bib29" class="ltx_ref">59</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" class="ltx_ref">60</a>\], Codex Security \[<a href="#bib.bib32" class="ltx_ref">24</a>\], BigSleep \[<a href="#bib.bib18" class="ltx_ref">79</a>\], XintCode \[<a href="#bib.bib20" class="ltx_ref">80</a>\], and XBOW \[<a href="#bib.bib19" class="ltx_ref">81</a>\] have used LLMs to uncover thousands of vulnerabilities in production systems. In contrast to direct LLM scanning, which is prohibitively expensive for continuous scanning and suffers from high false-positive rates \[<a href="#bib.bib68" class="ltx_ref">39</a>\], Antiproof uses efficient static detectors to continuously scan large systems and proofs of exploitability for automatic validation.

</div>

<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">

<span id="S7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vulnerability Validation.</span> Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) test generation has been extensively studied \[<a href="#bib.bib10" class="ltx_ref">33</a>\]. Recent works, including AnyPoC \[<a href="#bib.bib62" class="ltx_ref">30</a>\], FaultLine \[<a href="#bib.bib21" class="ltx_ref">31</a>\], and CVE-GENIE \[<a href="#bib.bib6" class="ltx_ref">32</a>\], leverage LLMs for proof-of-vulnerability test generation. Because these approaches automatically validate the PoV using LLM-as-a-judge verifiers or bug oracles such as memory sanitizers \[<a href="#bib.bib71" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib72" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib73" class="ltx_ref">49</a>\], they either are limited in vulnerability-class coverage or inherit LLM limitations such as hallucinations, reward hacking, and weaker performance on long-context reasoning \[<a href="#bib.bib66" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib68" class="ltx_ref">39</a>\]. Recent exploitability benchmarks such as ExploitBench \[<a href="#bib.bib28" class="ltx_ref">82</a>\] and ExploitGym \[<a href="#bib.bib27" class="ltx_ref">83</a>\] evaluate the ability of LLMs to exploit vulnerabilities, but focus on code execution from memory-safety vulnerabilities. Rather than relying on manual review or LLMs, Antiproof extends the notion of CTF-based validation \[<a href="#bib.bib83" class="ltx_ref">54</a>\] to prove attacker capabilities without a precise bug oracle. This shifts the manual review bottleneck from every vulnerability candidate to a small set of validation environments and oracles and allows Antiproof to automatically validate vulnerability classes beyond memory safety.

</div>

</div>

<div id="S8" class="section ltx_section">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VIII </span><span id="S8.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">

Scalable vulnerability discovery is critical to secure computer systems before attackers exploit them. In this paper, we have presented Antiproof, an end-to-end vulnerability discovery system for continuously scanning large-scale projects for vulnerability patterns with high recall and low discovery and validation costs. Antiproof uses LLMs to continually synthesize and refine static detectors for high-recall discovery and executable proofs of exploitability for automatic validation. We show that this novel approach outperforms existing baselines on two known vulnerability benchmarks, BountyBench and our curated KEVBench dataset. Evaluated on 50 widely deployed open-source projects, Antiproof generated 510 proofs of exploitability. Due to time constraints, we selected 100 findings for manual review and coordinated disclosure. To date, we have received 12 CVE assignments for vulnerabilities of critical or high severity, including remote code execution vulnerabilities that could lead to complete takeover of widely deployed LLM inference and training systems.

</div>

</div>

<div id="Sx1" class="section ltx_section">

## Ethics Considerations

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We recognize the dual-use risk of vulnerability discovery. To mitigate this risk, we manually review selected findings and coordinate disclosure of confirmed vulnerabilities with affected maintainers and vendors. When possible, we suggest patches or mitigations and allow affected parties sufficient time to develop and deploy fixes before public disclosure. We evaluate only on publicly available open-source projects and vulnerability benchmarks, and reproduce vulnerabilities only in local environments without affecting production systems. We do not collect personally identifiable information or sensitive data in this research. Our goal is to help defenders find and fix existing flaws before attackers exploit them.

</div>

</div>

<div id="A1" class="section ltx_appendix">

## <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Agent Prompts

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">

We show simplified excerpts from the system prompts for Antiproof’s LLM agents (<span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Synthesis</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environment Preparation</span>, <span id="A1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Environment Verifier</span>, and <span id="A1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Prover</span>) and the prompt used for the direct LLM-agent reference points. Bracketed ellipses mark omitted operational instructions.

## Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

- Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,))</span> button, located in the page header.

**Tip:** You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified <a href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues" class="ltx_ref" target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML" class="ltx_ref" target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" class="ltx_ref" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.
